Reference snippets:
[SB 18-661] Combustion leak (block) test. On 2010-2015 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.
[SM 3.7.7] Misfire under load from a tracked or fouled spark plug. Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire under load may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.
[SM-0484] Misfire while idle from a tracked or fouled spark plug. Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2010-2022. A single-cylinder misfire while idle may come from a spark plug with a cracked insulator, carbon tracking or an excessive gap. Remove the plug from the misfiring cylinder and compare it with one from a cylinder that is not misfiring. Check the gap against the underhood emissions label (typically 0.040-0.044 in). Repair: replace the spark plugs as a set.

Our family's 2017 compact crossover with the 2.4L and the automatic transmission, just past 160,506 miles. It bucks under load, like merging onto the highway, and the scan tool shows P0303. No problem at idle, rain or shine. Any idea which check to begin with?

Pull the spark plug from cylinder 3 and inspect it side by side with one from a cylinder that isn't misfiring, looking for a cracked insulator or carbon tracking and measuring its gap against the underhood emissions label, typically 0.040-0.044 in [SM 3.7.7]. With P0303 and bucking only under load on your 2.4L, that plug's condition is the right place to start.

[SM-9394] Stabilizer link inspection. Applies to vehicles with a front stabilizer bar, model years 2010-2015. With the vehicle on the ground so the suspension is loaded, grasp each stabilizer link and push and pull firmly. Watch both ball studs for play or a knock. Any free play, or a torn boot with grease loss, indicates a worn link. A short pry bar helps on stiff links.
[TSB-7161] Overheating at idle from a restricted radiator core. Applies to gasoline engines, model years 2011-2021. Scale or debris in the radiator core can make temperature climb at idle and in traffic. With the engine warm and the thermostat open, compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank using an infrared thermometer. A drop of 20-40 deg F is typical; a much smaller drop, or cold spots across the core, indicates restricted flow. Repair: flush or replace the radiator.

Shop ticket: 2014 hatchback, 1.6L, stick shift, odometer 67,696. Got stuck in a drive-through line and the temp gauge went almost to the red. Once I got back on the road it came down. It never runs hot at highway speed. One more thing: clunk from the front end, right side, on rough pavement. It definitely comes from the front, and it doesn't happen when turning sharply. Any idea which check to begin with?

With the 1.6L fully warm and the thermostat open, let it idle and use an infrared thermometer to compare the radiator inlet tank with the outlet tank, scanning across the core for cold spots; a drop of about 20-40 deg F is normal, while a much smaller drop or cold patches points to restricted flow [TSB-7161]. That pattern fits a gauge that climbs in a drive-through line but stays normal at highway speed.

With the engine idling and the AC switched on, confirm the condenser fan runs. Without airflow across the condenser at idle, high-side pressure rises. Repair: correct the fan circuit fault or replace the fan motor.
[TSB-1285] Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout. Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the steering wheel may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

I bought a used 2016 compact sedan with the 2.0L four-cylinder and automatic transmission; it shows 166,135 miles. The brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking. Can you point me to a good starting check?

Measure front rotor lateral runout by mounting a dial indicator to the knuckle, with the hub face clean and the lug nuts torqued to specification, setting the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotating the rotor one full turn [TSB-1285]. Runout must stay at or below 0.002 in, and a higher reading would match the pedal pulse and wheel shake you get braking from highway speed.

[SEC 19.12] Battery state-of-health test. Applies to midsize sedans, small crossovers and hatchbacks, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

That quick look will tell you far more than a guess before you spend money on any part.
